question: How many liters of wine, per person (age 15+), did Italians drink on average in 2024?
answer: ~42.7 liters
note: OIV (International Organisation of Vine and Wine) methodology, which counts population 15+; a lower "whole population" figure of ~26.3 L/person also circulates depending on methodology used.

question: What global rank does Italy hold for total volume of wine consumed (not per capita) in 2024?
answer: 3rd — about 2.23 billion liters, behind the United States (3.33 billion) and France (2.30 billion)
note: Industry reporting citing OIV/Statista-sourced 2024 consumption data.

question: What percentage of Sicily's red-grape vineyard area is planted with Nero d'Avola?
note: Same viticulture-of-Sicily sourcing as above.

question: How many DOC/DOCG wine designations does Sicily have in total?
answer: 24 (23 DOC + 1 DOCG)
note: Sicily's sole DOCG is Cerasuolo di Vittoria (the Nero d'Avola/Frappato blend); it covers just ~152 hectares of vineyard.

question: How many kilograms of pasta does the average Italian eat per year — the highest of any country?
note: International Pasta Organisation / AIDEPI 2024 figures; some sources round to 23–26 kg depending on year.

question: What percentage of Italy's pasta production is exported abroad?
answer: Nearly 60% (2.42 million tonnes, worth about €4 billion)
note: Italian Food/AIDEPI export data; top destinations are Germany, the US, the UK, France and Japan.

question: How many kilograms of pizza does the average Italian eat per year?
answer: ~7.6 kg per person
note: Consumption-statistics aggregators citing national dietary data; for comparison, Norway's per-capita figure is actually higher (~11.4 kg).

question: What percentage of Italians drink coffee at all?
note: Same coffee-culture consumption surveys; ~74% drink it daily.

question: How many separate PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) olive oil labels does Sicily hold?
answer: 6 — Monti Iblei, Valli Trapanesi, Val di Mazara, Monte Etna, Valle del Belice, and Valdemone
note: Regional PDO registry as reported in Sicilian food-trade sources.

question: At its narrowest point, how wide is the Strait of Messina separating Sicily from mainland Italy?
answer: 3.1 km (between Torre Faro and Villa San Giovanni)
note: Standard geographic references; at the city of Messina itself the strait widens to about 5.1 km.

question: How many countries border the Mediterranean Sea?
note: Standard geographic/political reference (includes Italy, France, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Morocco, Algeria, and others).

question: Into how many administrative regions is Italy divided?
note: Standard constitutional/geographic reference; 5 of the 20 hold special autonomous status (including Sicily itself).

question: How many main islands make up the Aeolian archipelago north of Sicily?
answer: 7 — Lipari, Vulcano, Salina, Stromboli, Filicudi, Alicudi and Panarea
note: UNESCO World Heritage listing (inscribed December 2000); plus five smaller islets.

question: How long is the Cavagrande del Cassibile canyon, near Avola/Noto?
answer: ~10 km long
note: Sicilian nature-reserve reference sources; considered the largest natural canyon in Europe.

question: What is Mount Etna's diameter at its base?
answer: ~35 km
note: Same volcanological reference sources.

question: What magnitude was the catastrophic 1693 earthquake that destroyed Noto and much of southeastern Sicily?
answer: An estimated magnitude 7.4 — the most powerful earthquake in recorded Italian history
note: Seismological/historical reference sources (Wikipedia's well-cited 1693 Sicily earthquake entry, cross-referenced against academic summaries).

question: How many towns make up the "Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto" UNESCO World Heritage listing, and in what year was it inscribed?
answer: 8 towns, inscribed in 2002 — Caltagirone, Militello Val di Catania, Catania, Modica, Noto, Palazzolo Acreide, Ragusa and Scicli
note: UNESCO World Heritage Centre official listing (site #1024).

question: For how many years did the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies exist, before Italian unification?
note: Historical reference sources; ended when Garibaldi's conquest led to a plebiscite joining the Kingdom of Sardinia.

question: How many major Greek temples make up the Valley of the Temples at Agrigento?
answer: 8 (built roughly 510–430 BC)
note: Archaeological/UNESCO-site reference sources; some sources count as few as 7 or as many as 9 depending on whether smaller ruins are included.

question: How many years was Noto Cathedral closed for reconstruction after its 1996 collapse?
answer: 11 years — it reopened on June 15, 2007
note: Same source as above; reconstruction work itself ran 1999–2007.

question: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are located specifically in Sicily?
answer: 7 — the Aeolian Islands, Mount Etna, Villa Romana del Casale, Syracuse & the Necropolis of Pantalica, the Val di Noto Baroque towns, the Arab-Norman sites of Palermo/Monreale/Cefalù, and Agrigento's archaeological park
note: Sicily-focused UNESCO travel/heritage reference sources, cross-checked against the official Italy list.

question: How many of those are three-star restaurants?
answer: 15 (plus 38 two-star and 341 one-star restaurants)
note: Same official 2026 Michelin Guide Italy breakdown; 25 restaurants were newly starred that year.

question: What was Italy's total fertility rate in 2024 — one of the lowest in the world?
answer: 1.18 births per woman
note: Demographic statistics well below the EU average of 1.38.

question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
note: One pumps blood to the body, two pump blood to the gills (Britannica, Smithsonian).

question: How many years can a tardigrade ("water bear") survive without any water at all?
answer: Up to about 30 years
note: Achieved via cryptobiosis — it expels its water, curls into a "tun," and rehydrates back to life in hours (NSF, ScienceAlert).

question: How many hearts does an earthworm have?
answer: 10 (five pairs of "aortic arches" that act like hearts)
note: They're not true hearts, but muscular vessels that pump blood in a wave-like rhythm (A-Z Animals).

question: How long can a cockroach survive after losing its head?
answer: Roughly 1–2 weeks
note: It breathes through holes in its body segments, not its head, and eventually dies of dehydration, not decapitation (Scientific American).

question: How many eyes does a honeybee have?
answer: 5 (two large compound eyes plus three small simple eyes called ocelli)
note: The ocelli sit in a triangle atop the head and help bees orient using sunlight (IFLScience).

question: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?
answer: 7 — the same number as a human
note: Each giraffe vertebra is just far longer (up to 10 inches) rather than more numerous (Snopes, Save Giraffes Now).

question: How many hours a day does a koala typically sleep?
answer: 18 to 22 hours
note: Their eucalyptus diet is low-energy and mildly toxic, requiring extended digestion/rest (Australian Koala Foundation).

question: Dolphins can stay alert for roughly how many days straight without normal sleep?
answer: At least 15 days
note: They sleep with only half their brain at a time (unihemispheric sleep), keeping one eye open (Smithsonian Magazine).

question: How many stomach compartments does a cow have?
answer: 4 (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum) — but it's technically one stomach, not four separate ones
note: The rumen acts as a giant fermentation vat for digesting tough plant fiber (Britannica).

question: How many muscles does a cat have in each ear?
note: That lets each ear rotate up to 180 degrees independently — compare 3 in a human ear (Catster).

question: How long can some land snails hibernate (estivate) in a single stretch when conditions are bad?
answer: Up to about 3 years
note: They seal themselves in their shell with a mucus layer to conserve moisture (A-Z Animals).

question: Roughly what's the ratio of chickens to humans on Earth right now?
answer: About 3-to-1 (roughly 26 billion chickens vs. ~8.2 billion people)
note: Chickens are the most numerous bird on the planet by a huge margin (The Humane League, Carnegie Museum).

question: A centipede's name implies 100 legs — how many pairs of legs can centipede species actually have?
answer: Anywhere from 15 to 177 pairs (always an odd number of pairs, so never exactly 100 legs)
note: The common house centipede has just 15 pairs = 30 legs total (Snopes).

question: How many human beings have ever walked on the Moon?
answer: 12 — all men, all part of NASA's Apollo missions (1969–1972)
note: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were first; Eugene Cernan was the last, in 1972 (Space.com).

question: About how many minutes does it take sunlight to reach Earth?
answer: About 8 minutes 20 seconds
note: Based on Earth's average distance of ~150 million km from the Sun (BBC Sky at Night).

question: How many facial muscles does it typically take to produce a smile?
answer: About 10–12 for an average smile (a big toothy grin can engage up to 43)
note: There's no single agreed number since smile types vary so much (HowStuffWorks).

question: About how many liters of saliva does the average adult produce in a day?
answer: Roughly 1–2 liters
note: Estimates across studies range from about 0.5 to 1.5+ liters (Cleveland Clinic).

question: About how fast does human scalp hair grow per month?
answer: About half an inch (1.25 cm)
note: Growth rate varies notably by ethnicity and genetics (American Academy of Dermatology, via LiveScience).

question: About how many liters of air can the average pair of adult lungs hold at full capacity?
answer: About 6 liters
note: Normal breathing only uses a small fraction of total lung capacity (American Lung Association-adjacent sources).

question: Roughly what percentage of an adult male's body weight is made up of skeleton?
answer: About 14% (roughly 10–12% for adult females)
note: A living skeleton weighs more than a "dry" one due to marrow, blood vessels, and other tissue (BioNumbers database).

question: How tall was Robert Wadlow, the tallest person in verified medical history?
answer: 8 feet 11.1 inches (2.72 m)
note: Caused by a pituitary condition; he was last measured in 1940 (Guinness World Records).

question: How many wives did England's King Henry VIII have?
note: Immortalized in the rhyme "divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived" (Historic Royal Palaces).

question: How much honey does a single honeybee produce in its entire lifetime?
answer: About 1/12 of a teaspoon
note: It takes roughly 12 worker bees' lifetime output to make just one teaspoon of honey (Carolina Honeybees, Bee Professor).

question: What's the current men's 100m world record time, set by Usain Bolt?
answer: 9.58 seconds
note: Set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin.

question: How many total Olympic medals did swimmer Michael Phelps win across his career?
answer: 28 (including 23 gold — both the most of any Olympian ever)
note: He won a record 8 gold medals at a single Games (Beijing 2008) (Olympics.com).

question: How long did the longest professional tennis match in history last?
answer: 11 hours 5 minutes, spread across 3 days
note: John Isner beat Nicolas Mahut 70–68 in the final set at Wimbledon 2010 (Guinness World Records).

question: How many time zones does Russia span — the most of any country?
note: 10 of them are contiguous; the 11th covers the Kaliningrad exclave (Wikipedia/Time in Russia).

question: About how many hours per day does the average person globally spend on their smartphone?
answer: Around 3 hours 52 minutes globally (US average runs closer to 4.5–5+ hours)
note: Figures continue climbing year over year across most countries (Priori Data, Demandsage).

question: A captive "immortal jellyfish" studied by a Japanese scientist reverted from adult back to its baby polyp stage and regrew into an adult again — how many times did it do this over about two years?
answer: 11 times
note: Species is Turritopsis dohrnii; the process is called transdifferentiation. Researcher Shin Kubota's colony repeated the cycle 11 times (Wikipedia, citing published observations).

question: How long is an elephant's pregnancy (gestation period)?
answer: About 18 to 22 months (up to nearly 2 years) — the longest of any mammal
note: Compare a human's roughly 9 months (Wikipedia).

question: How wide can a giant squid's eyeball get — the largest eye of any living creature?
answer: Up to about 27 cm (11 inches) in diameter, with a pupil around 9 cm (3.5 in) across
note: Only extinct ichthyosaurs are known to have had larger eyes (Wikipedia).

question: How many light-years away is Proxima Centauri, the closest known star to our Sun (besides the Sun itself)?
answer: About 4.25 light-years
note: That's still around 25 trillion miles / 40 trillion km — humanity's fastest spacecraft would take tens of thousands of years to get there (Wikipedia, Gaia Data Release 3).

question: What's the largest hailstone (by diameter) ever officially recorded?
answer: 20 cm (7.9 inches) across — nearly the size of a basketball — which fell in Vivian, South Dakota, on 23 July 2010
note: A separate hailstone that fell in Bangladesh in 1986 holds the weight record at 1.02 kg (2.2 lb) (Wikipedia — Hail).

question: A common swift can stay continuously airborne — eating, sleeping, even mating on the wing — for up to how long without ever landing?
answer: Up to about 10 months at a stretch
note: Non-breeding individuals only touch down again to nest; their max horizontal flight speed is about 112 km/h (69 mph) (Wikipedia — Common swift).

question: Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system. How tall is it compared to Mount Everest?
answer: About 21.3 km (13.2 miles) tall — roughly 2.5 times the height of Mount Everest above sea level
note: Measured via NASA's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (Wikipedia — Olympus Mons).

question: Naked mole-rats are tiny (30-35 grams) but live remarkably long for a rodent — what's the longest recorded lifespan for one?
answer: Over 37 years — by far the longest-lived rodent known (the next-longest, the African porcupine, tops out around 28 years)
note: They're also famously resistant to cancer and largely immune to pain from acid or chili-pepper burns (Wikipedia — Naked mole-rat).

question: The wandering (snowy) albatross has the longest confirmed wingspan of any living bird — how wide?
answer: Up to 3.7 metres (12 ft 2 in) tip to tip
note: Unverified reports claim specimens over 5 metres, but 3.7 m is the confirmed record (Wikipedia — Wandering albatross).

question: What's the longest a total solar eclipse can theoretically last, from start to end of totality?
answer: 7 minutes 32 seconds maximum — the longest actually observed in the 20th century was 7 minutes 8 seconds, in 1955
note: In 1973, scientists aboard a Concorde jet chased the Moon's shadow and stretched their observed totality to about 74 minutes (Wikipedia — Solar eclipse).

question: The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the largest tides on Earth. What's the biggest tidal range ever recorded there?
answer: 21.6 metres (71 feet) — recorded in October 1869, when a storm surge coincided with an unusually high spring tide
note: The typical daily tidal range there is still a massive 16 metres (52 ft) (Wikipedia — Bay of Fundy).

question: What's the record length for a king cobra, the world's longest venomous snake?
answer: 5.85 metres (19.2 feet) — nearly 4 metres longer than the average adult human is tall
note: Its venom glands can hold enough neurotoxin to deliver an unusually large dose per bite (Wikipedia — King cobra).

question: What's the smallest bat species in the world, and how much does it weigh?
answer: Kitti's hog-nosed bat ("bumblebee bat"), just 29-33 mm long and weighing about 2 grams — roughly the weight of a small paperclip
note: It's a contender for smallest mammal on Earth by body length, though the Etruscan shrew may be lighter by mass (Wikipedia — Bumblebee bat).

question: How long can a giant Gippsland earthworm — a real species native to Australia — grow?
answer: Up to 3 metres (10 feet) long, though they're typically closer to 1 metre
note: They're so large you can reportedly hear them squelching underground and have to dig several feet down to find them (Wikipedia — Giant Gippsland earthworm).

question: The lion's mane jellyfish has the longest tentacles of any known animal — how long can they stretch?
answer: Up to 36.6 metres (120 feet) in the longest documented specimen — longer than a blue whale
note: Most trail a still-impressive 30 metres (100 ft) or more (Wikipedia — Lion's mane jellyfish).

question: Inside Mexico's "Cave of Crystals" (Naica Cave), some of the largest natural crystals ever found were discovered — how big was the largest?
answer: 11.4 metres (37.4 feet) long and weighing about 12 tonnes
note: The cave itself was so hot and humid (up to 58°C/136°F) that explorers could only survive inside for around 10 minutes wearing special cooling suits (Wikipedia — Cave of the Crystals).

question: How long is a single day (one full rotation) on Jupiter, the solar system's biggest planet?
answer: Just 9.93 hours — under 10 hours, despite Jupiter being over 11 times wider than Earth
note: Jupiter's extremely fast spin is also why it visibly bulges at its equator (Wikipedia — Jupiter).

question: In some deep-sea anglerfish species, males are dramatically smaller than females and permanently fuse to them. In the most extreme known species, how much bigger is the female than the tiny male?
answer: Roughly 7-8 times longer — males mature at just 6.2-7.3 mm, females at about 50.5 mm (Photocorynus spiniceps)
note: The male bites onto the female and eventually fuses into her body, living the rest of his life as an attached sperm-producing parasite (Wikipedia — Anglerfish).

question: What's the largest snowflake ever recorded?
answer: 38 cm (15 inches) wide, reportedly observed at Fort Keogh, Montana, in January 1887
note: Guinness World Records lists it, though the claim is well outside normally documented snowflake sizes of 7.5-10 cm and hasn't been independently re-verified (Wikipedia — Snowflake).

question: How many days did it take Avatar to become the fastest film ever to reach $1 billion at the worldwide box office (on its original 2009-2010 release)?
answer: 19 days
note: Wikipedia "Avatar (2009 film)" — it went on to become the first film ever to cross $2 billion, on January 31, 2010.

question: Titanic (1997) cost about $200 million to make — roughly how many times over did it earn that back at the worldwide box office?
answer: About 11 times — it grossed $2.264 billion worldwide
note: Wikipedia "Titanic (1997 film)".

question: How many total films has Marvel Studios released in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) as of 2026?
answer: 37 films
note: Wikipedia "List of Marvel Cinematic Universe films" — combined they've grossed over $32.4 billion worldwide, making it by far the highest-grossing film franchise ever.

question: How many theatrical Star Wars films have been released in total (Skywalker Saga plus anthology/spin-off films)?
answer: 13 films
note: Wikipedia "Star Wars" — combined they've grossed over $10 billion, making Star Wars the third-highest-grossing film franchise ever.

question: What's the record for most Academy Awards (Oscars) won by a single film?
answer: 11 — a three-way tie between Ben-Hur (1959), Titanic (1997), and The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003)
note: Wikipedia "List of Academy Award records". Notably, Return of the King won all 11 categories it was nominated in — a perfect sweep.

question: Who holds the record for the most Academy Awards (Oscars) won by any individual, across all categories, in history?
answer: Walt Disney, with 22 wins
note: Wikipedia "List of Academy Award records" — from a record 59 nominations, spanning animated shorts, documentaries, and special awards.

question: Who holds the record for most Grammy Awards ever won by a single person?
answer: Beyoncé, with 35 wins
note: Wikipedia "List of Grammy Award records" — conductor Sir Georg Solti is second with 31.

question: How many seasons and episodes does The Simpsons have, making it the longest-running scripted primetime series in US TV history?
answer: 37 seasons and 808 episodes (and still airing)
note: Wikipedia "List of longest-running scripted American primetime television series" — it premiered December 17, 1989.

question: How many Billboard Hot 100 #1 singles has Mariah Carey had as a solo artist — the most of any solo act in history?
answer: 19 number-one singles
note: Wikipedia "Mariah Carey".

question: Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" holds a Billboard chart record — what is it?
answer: The longest-running #1 single of all time on the Billboard Hot 100, with 22 total weeks at number one (accumulated across multiple holiday seasons)
note: Wikipedia "Mariah Carey" — it had also sold over 16 million copies worldwide as of 2017, making it the best-selling holiday single by a woman.

question: Who holds the record for the most Academy Award acting nominations of all time?
answer: Meryl Streep, with 21 nominations (and 3 wins)
note: Wikipedia "Meryl Streep".

question: How many official James Bond films have been released in total (including the two non-Eon productions)?
answer: 27 films
note: Wikipedia "James Bond (film series)" — 25 from the main Eon Productions series plus 2 outside it (1967's "Casino Royale" and 1983's "Never Say Never Again"). Combined nominal box office is about $7.8 billion.

question: How many Grammy Awards did Michael Jackson win across his career?
answer: 13 Grammy Awards
note: Wikipedia "Michael Jackson" — he's also sold an estimated 500+ million records worldwide as a solo artist, one of the best-selling music artists ever.

question: How many Grammy Awards has Adele won across her career?
answer: 16 Grammy Awards
note: Wikipedia "Adele" — alongside 12 Brit Awards, an Oscar, an Emmy and a Golden Globe (an "EGOT"-adjacent haul).

question: Beyoncé holds the record for most Grammy Awards won in a single night by a female artist — how many did she win at the 2010 ceremony?
answer: 6 Grammy Awards in one night
note: Wikipedia "Beyoncé" — for the album "I Am... Sasha Fierce" and the song "Single Ladies," among others.

question: How much did a first-class US postage stamp cost in 1900?
answer: 2 cents
note: Wikipedia, "History of United States postage rates" (rate set in 1885, held through the 1910s).

question: How much did a first-class US postage stamp cost in 1970?
answer: 6 cents (it had just risen to 6 cents in January 1968; it jumped to 8 cents in May 1971)
note: Wikipedia, "History of United States postage rates."

question: Hungary's pengő suffered the worst hyperinflation ever recorded, after WWII. At its peak, prices doubled roughly every how many hours?
answer: About every 15 hours
note: Wikipedia, "Pengő" — the largest banknote ever issued anywhere was Hungary's 100 quintillion (10^20) pengő note.

question: The Channel Tunnel between the UK and France went massively over budget. By roughly what percentage did final costs exceed the original budget?
answer: About 80% over budget (final cost £4.65 billion vs. an original £2.6 billion budget)
note: Wikipedia, "Channel Tunnel."

question: When Coca-Cola first went on sale in 1886, how much did a glass cost?
answer: 5 cents
note: Wikipedia, "Coca-Cola" — sold at Jacob's Pharmacy in Atlanta.

question: What was the US federal minimum wage when it was first established in 1938?
answer: 25 cents per hour (about $5.72 in 2025 dollars)
note: Wikipedia, "Minimum wage in the United States," Fair Labor Standards Act.

question: What is the current US federal minimum wage, unchanged since 2009?
answer: $7.25 per hour
note: Wikipedia, "Minimum wage in the United States."

question: A Big Mac in the US cost how much in July 2008, according to the Economist's Big Mac Index?
note: Wikipedia, "Big Mac Index."

question: In April 2020, US oil prices did something that had never happened before in recorded history — they went negative. What was the lowest price reached, per barrel?
answer: About -$37 per barrel (traders paid buyers to take oil off their hands due to a storage crunch)
note: Wikipedia, "2020 Russia-Saudi Arabia oil price war."

question: The world's first commercial movie theater opened in New York in 1894. What did it cost to get in and watch a row of films?
answer: 25 cents
note: Wikipedia, "Movie theater" — about $9.30 in today's money.

question: What was the average price of a movie ticket in the US in 2013?
note: Wikipedia, "Movie theater."

question: When Netflix separated its streaming and DVD plans in 2011, what was the monthly price for streaming?
answer: $7.99 per month
note: Wikipedia, "Netflix."

question: The Apollo Guidance Computer that flew astronauts to the Moon ran at what clock speed?
answer: 2.048 MHz (about 1.024 MHz for actual processing)
note: Wikipedia — Apollo Guidance Computer. It had just 2,048 words of RAM and 36,864 words of ROM, roughly comparable to a 1970s home computer.

question: Inside the LHC, protons are accelerated to what percentage of the speed of light?
answer: About 99.9999991% of the speed of light (roughly 3.1 m/s slower than light itself)
note: Wikipedia — Large Hadron Collider.

question: The James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror is how wide?
answer: 6.5 metres (about 21 feet) in diameter, made of 18 gold-coated hexagonal segments
note: Wikipedia — James Webb Space Telescope. It operates below 50 K (−223°C) and cost about $9.7 billion total.

question: The Human Genome Project took how many years and roughly how much money to sequence the first human genome (completed 2003)?
answer: 13 years (1990–2003) and about $2.7 billion
note: Wikipedia — Human Genome Project.

question: Hubble Space Telescope's primary mirror is how wide?
answer: 2.4 metres (7 ft 10 in) in diameter
note: Wikipedia — Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, it orbits roughly 540 km above Earth.

question: How many satellites orbit roughly 20,200 km above Earth to make up the operational GPS constellation?
answer: Around 31 operational satellites (minimum design was 24)
note: Wikipedia — Global Positioning System.

question: Frontier, the first supercomputer to break the "exascale" barrier (2022), can perform how many operations per second at peak?
answer: 2.055 exaFLOPS — over 2 quintillion calculations per second
note: Wikipedia — Frontier (supercomputer).

question: When Chile's Extremely Large Telescope is completed, how wide will its primary mirror be — nearly 4x the size of any existing optical telescope?
answer: 39.3 metres (129 ft) in diameter, built from 798 hexagonal segments
note: Wikipedia — Extremely Large Telescope.

question: How many years passed between the Higgs boson's theoretical prediction (1964) and its experimental confirmation at the LHC?
answer: 48 years — the particle was confirmed on 4 July 2012
note: Wikipedia — Higgs boson.

question: By 2018, roughly how many MOSFET transistors (a specific transistor type) had been manufactured in total — making it the most-produced human-made object in history?
note: Wikipedia — Transistor.

question: What is the power capacity of the world's most powerful wind turbine currently in operation (the DEC H26-313 in Fuzhou, China)?
answer: 26 megawatts — a single turbine that can power tens of thousands of homes
note: Wikipedia — Wind turbine.

question: How fast did the Concorde supersonic jet cruise, cutting a Paris-to-New York flight down from 7-8 hours to how long?
answer: Mach 2.02 (about 2,150 km/h / 1,330 mph) — cutting transatlantic flights to under 3.5 hours
note: Wikipedia — Concorde.

question: What percentage of international internet data traffic actually travels through undersea fiber-optic cables, rather than satellites?
answer: About 99% — satellites carry well under 1% of global data traffic
note: Wikipedia — Submarine communications cable.

question: The world's first successful photograph was taken in 1826 by Nicéphore Niépce. How long did the exposure need to be to capture it?
answer: At least 8 hours, and probably several days
note: Wikipedia — Photography. Compare to modern smartphone cameras, which can capture a photo in a fraction of a millisecond.

question: In 1969, the first message was sent over ARPANET (the internet's precursor) between UCLA and Stanford. What were the only two letters that made it through before the system crashed?
answer: "lo" — the programmer was trying to type "login" when the receiving computer crashed after the second letter
note: Wikipedia — ARPANET. The full connection was completed about an hour later.
_backup_reason: answer is not a guessable number

question: El Capitan, which became the world's fastest supercomputer in late 2024, reaches what peak performance?
answer: 2.821 exaFLOPS (2.821 quintillion calculations per second) at peak — noticeably faster than Frontier's 2.055 exaFLOPS
note: Wikipedia — El Capitan (supercomputer). Housed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

question: The first COVID-19 vaccines were developed and authorized in a record-breaking amount of time — how many months did it take, from the virus's genome being sequenced to an approved vaccine?
answer: About 11 months (genome sequenced January 2020; first vaccine authorized December 2020)
note: Wikipedia — COVID-19 vaccine. Previously, the fastest vaccine ever developed (mumps) had taken about 4 years.

question: In 1965, cosmonaut Alexei Leonov performed the first-ever spacewalk. How long was he outside the spacecraft?
answer: 12 minutes and 9 seconds
note: Wikipedia — Alexei Leonov. His spacesuit ballooned so much in the vacuum of space that he had to partially deflate it just to squeeze back through the airlock.

question: The shortest laser pulse ever created by scientists — recognized by the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics — lasted how long?
answer: 43 attoseconds (43 quintillionths of a second)
note: Wikipedia — Attosecond. Short enough to capture the movement of electrons inside atoms; there are more attoseconds in one second than seconds that have passed since the Big Bang.

question: The Very Large Array radio telescope in New Mexico can reposition its antennas along Y-shaped rail tracks to change its resolution. How many antennas does it use at once, and how long is each arm of the array?
answer: 27 antennas (plus 1 spare), each 25 metres wide, spread along arms up to 21 km (13 miles) long
note: Wikipedia — Very Large Array. Its dishes can be reconfigured into four different array sizes depending on what astronomers need to observe.

question: The camera at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, built to photograph the entire visible sky every few nights, has what resolution — the largest camera ever built?
answer: 3.2 gigapixels, built from a mosaic of 189 separate 16-megapixel sensors
note: Wikipedia — Vera C. Rubin Observatory. That's roughly 200 times the resolution of a typical smartphone camera.
